claim: COCO/BBOB benchmarking platform bases performance assessment on runtime (function evaluations to reach a target quality value) rather than on raw/magnitude quality-indicator scores, because runtime is 'the only available measure with a generic, meaningful, and quantitative interpretation.'
stance_target: min-max normalization of raw score magnitudes is a weaker aggregation choice than runtime/target-based measures in benchmark design
scope_conditions: Black-box numerical optimization benchmarking (COCO/BBOB platform), general methodological argument not specific to any single algorithm
quoted_support: We argue that runtime is the only available measure with a generic, meaningful, and quantitative interpretation. In the context of black-box optimization, the runtime to reach a target value, measured in number of function evaluations, satisfies all requirements.

claim: A performance measure should assume a wide variation of values and not cluster in a narrow range (e.g., 0.98 to 1.0), because narrow-range magnitude measures lose interpretability -- an implicit critique of raw-score/min-max-style measures that can compress most entrants into a narrow band.
stance_target: magnitude-based normalization is fragile when compared entities cluster near the top or bottom of the observed range
scope_conditions: General requirements for performance measures in black-box optimization benchmarking
quoted_support: assuming a wide variation of values such that, for example, typical values do not only range between 0.98 and 1.0

claim: Fixed-budget (raw quality-indicator value) comparisons between algorithms are explicitly rejected as not quantitatively interpretable, because a two-times-smaller indicator value has no a priori meaningful interpretation of relative difficulty, whereas fixed-target (runtime) comparisons directly support ratio statements like 'Algorithm A is two times faster.'
stance_target: raw magnitude/score-based aggregation (analogous to min-max normalizing raw cell means) lacks quantitative interpretability compared to a runtime/target-based measure
scope_conditions: COCO black-box optimization benchmarking methodology, fixed-budget vs fixed-target framework
quoted_support: The fixed-budget approach (vertical cut) does not give quantitatively interpretable data: the observation that Algorithm A reaches a quality indicator value that is, say, two times smaller than the one reached by Algorithm B has in general no interpretable meaning, mainly because there is no a priori way to determine how much more difficult it is to reach an indicator value that is two times smaller.

claim: Averaging runtime (aRT) across problem instances is explicitly stated to be dominated/distorted by a single outlier instance, which is why COCO restricts averaging to instances of the same function/dimension/target precision and uses geometric (log-space) averaging when aggregating across different functions or precisions.
stance_target: arithmetic mean-based aggregation (the basis of the mean cell values that get min-max normalized) is fragile to a single outlier/extreme instance dominating the statistic
scope_conditions: COCO aRT (average runtime) statistic, aggregation over problem instances
quoted_support: Taking the average is meaningful only if each instance obeys a similar distribution without heavy tail. If one instance is considerably harder than the others, the average is dominated by this instance. For this reason we do not average runtimes from different functions or different target precisions, which however could be done if the logarithm is taken first (geometric average).

claim: Empirical distribution functions (ECDFs) are preferred over single-number aggregates (like averages) partly because they display unlabeled data without losing information and remain meaningful under monotonic transformation of the underlying data, unlike an average which collapses to one dominated statistic.
stance_target: single-scalar aggregation (e.g., min-max normalized mean) sacrifices robustness/information relative to full-distribution displays
scope_conditions: COCO empirical distribution function (ECDF) aggregation methodology
quoted_support: Empirical cumulative distribution functions are a universal way to display unlabeled data in a condensed way without losing information. They allow unconstrained aggregation, because each data point remains separately displayed, and they remain entirely meaningful under transformation of the data (e.g. taking the logarithm).

claim: COCO explicitly warns that with only ~15 (or fewer) instances/runs per problem, apparent large effects can lack statistical significance -- e.g., 4/15 successes is not statistically significant against 0/15 successes at the 5% level -- directly analogous to concerns about small-N (e.g., 9-cell) statistics.
stance_target: small sample sizes (comparable order of magnitude to 9 experimental cells) can produce apparently large effects that are not statistically distinguishable from noise
scope_conditions: COCO simulated-restart runtime aggregation with K approx 15 independent instances
quoted_support: If only few or no successes have been observed, we can see large effects without statistical significance. Namely, 4/15 successes are not statistically significant against 0/15 successes on a 5%-level.
